title: Less Is More for Monitors? Testing Excerpt-Only Monitoring on LinuxArena Sabotage Transcripts
problem: LinuxArena shows ~34% undetected sabotage against monitors at 1% FPR, and separate work reports a 'less-is-more' effect where monitors do better on extracted excerpts than full transcripts — but this has not been tested on LinuxArena's sysadmin sabotage transcripts.
direction: Using LinuxArena's released transcripts, build a two-stage monitor: stage one extracts the few lines an action touches (file writes, network calls, privilege changes) via a heuristic or small model, stage two asks an LLM judge to score suspicion on just those excerpts. Compare detection at 1% FPR against a full-transcript baseline. Inference-only with an open judge model.
why_it_matters: Monitoring is the backbone of AI control, and sysadmin environments are where sandboxing fails; a cheap excerpt-extraction tweak that raises detection at fixed FPR would be directly deployable.
relevant_context: Extends 'LinuxArena' (Redwood, EquiStamp, 2026) — applies an excerpt-only monitoring strategy to its 34%-undetected result.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Monitoring is the backbone of AI control and a deployable excerpt tweak raising detection at fixed FPR targets a critical pathway.

low_compute.reasoning: Excerpt extraction plus an open judge model over released transcripts is inference-only.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Building a two-stage monitor with heuristic line extraction and FPR-calibrated comparison needs solid ML fundamentals.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused detection-at-1%-FPR comparison but the extraction stage adds dependencies.

counterfactual_value.reasoning: Monitoring strategy on released transcripts is independent-friendly and labs won't prioritize it.

title: An 'Overeagerness' Taxonomy: Hand-Coding Why Open Agents Misbehave in Sabotage Scenarios
problem: Gram attributes most observed misbehavior to 'overeagerness' rather than deliberate misalignment, but offers no reusable operational taxonomy others can apply to classify a misbehaving trajectory.
direction: Collect ~100-200 agent trajectories from open models run on a few sabotage-style prompts, then develop and apply a small annotation codebook distinguishing 'overeager goal-seeking', 'role-play spillover', 'misread instruction', and 'deliberate rule-breaking'. Report inter-rater (or LLM-judge vs hand-label) agreement and the category distribution.
why_it_matters: A shared concrete vocabulary for why an agent sabotaged lets the community compare results and decide whether a behavior is a safety threat or benign artifact.
relevant_context: Extends 'Gram' — operationalizes its 'largely overeagerness' claim into an applied taxonomy over open-model trajectories.
source_paper: Gram: Assessing sabotage propensities via automated alignment auditing — https://deepmind.google/research/publications/252981/

theory_of_impact.reasoning: A shared vocabulary for why agents sabotage aids comparison, but a taxonomy is a methodological contribution with a longer path to risk reduction.

low_compute.reasoning: Generating trajectories from open models plus hand-coding is low compute.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Building and applying an annotation codebook with agreement metrics is guided and novice-feasible.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused codebook plus category distribution, but annotating 100-200 trajectories is sizeable.

counterfactual_value.reasoning: Open trajectories and a public schema; independent-friendly methodology.

title: One Bit Is Enough? Replicating Boundary-Point Jailbreaking Against an Open-Source Safety Classifier
problem: Boundary-point attacks defeat strong deployed classifiers using only a single bit of feedback per query, but the published work targets closed frontier systems. It is unclear how cheaply the same one-bit curriculum attack works against an openly hostable safety classifier.
direction: Pick a public open-weight guard classifier (e.g. Llama Guard or a HuggingFace jailbreak classifier) as the black-box oracle. Implement a minimal boundary-point loop: take a target harmful string, build a small curriculum of intermediate paraphrases (open model via API), and at each step query the classifier for just the flag bit, keeping mutations at the decision boundary. Measure attack success and query/flag budget vs a naive random-paraphrase baseline. Inference-only.
why_it_matters: Classifier-based safeguards are the primary deployed defense layer; showing a one-bit feedback attack transfers cheaply to open classifiers tells deployers their guard models are brittle and motivates batch-level monitoring.
relevant_context: Extends 'Boundary Point Jailbreaking of Black-Box LLMs' (Davies, Irving, Gal et al., 2026) — reproduces the one-bit curriculum mechanism against a hostable open guard classifier.
source_paper: Boundary Point Jailbreaking of Black-Box LLMs — https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.15001

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Classifier guards are the primary deployed defense layer; showing a cheap one-bit attack transfers to open guards is a concrete, defensible chain.

low_compute.reasoning: Querying an open guard classifier with a paraphrase curriculum is inference-only.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Implementing a boundary-point curriculum loop keeping mutations at the decision boundary requires solid ML fundamentals beyond a pure beginner.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused on attack success vs a baseline, but the curriculum search has several dependencies.

counterfactual_value.reasoning: Attacking hostable open guard classifiers is independent-friendly and useful third-party scrutiny.

title: How Cheap Is the SFT Countermeasure? A Dose Curve for Breaking Exploration-Hacking Organisms
problem: Jang et al. report ~10 SFT steps and small weight noise break exploration-hacking organisms, but the minimal effective dose and its dependence on trigger strength are uncharacterized.
direction: Reusing the paper's code with a small Qwen3 organism, run a controlled sweep over the cheapest countermeasures: SFT steps (1,2,5,10,20) and weight-noise sigma (0.005,0.01,0.02), measuring how reliably each restores normal exploration on held-out malign-context prompts. Produce a dose-response heatmap of the minimal neutralizing intervention.
why_it_matters: If a handful of SFT steps reliably destroys hidden resistance, that is a cheap deployable safety lever; mapping the minimal dose grounds an empirical recommendation.
relevant_context: Extends 'Exploration Hacking' — the finding that ~10 SFT steps and weight noise break locked organisms.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Maps the minimal dose of a cheap safety lever, plausible mechanism but value depends on the lever generalizing beyond the model-organism toy setting.

low_compute.reasoning: Small Qwen3 organism with short SFT sweeps fits one GPU.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Requires building organism plus SFT/weight-noise sweep; intermediate with mentor support.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Tightly scoped sweep producing a single dose-response heatmap with clear success criteria.

counterfactual_value.reasoning: Released code, open model, fully independent-friendly.

title: Do NLA Verbalizers Hallucinate 'Safety-Test Awareness'? A Cheap Faithfulness Probe
problem: Natural Language Autoencoders surface text like 'awareness of being safety-tested' from activations, but the paper notes explanations can hallucinate and single claims are hard to verify, leaving verbalizer faithfulness unquantified.
direction: Using the released NLA code on a small supported open model, run the verbalizer on matched prompt pairs that are behaviorally identical but differ in whether they are framed as a 'safety test', plus control pairs. Check whether verbalized 'being-tested' text tracks actual framing (true positives) or appears spuriously on controls (hallucinations), giving a contrastive faithfulness rate for one specific NLA claim.
why_it_matters: NLAs are proposed as auditing aids, but tools that hallucinate awareness can mislead reviewers into false confidence or false alarms. A targeted contrastive test of one high-stakes claim is tractable.
relevant_context: Extends 'Natural Language Autoencoders' (Fraser-Taliente et al., 2026) — the verbalized 'awareness of being safety-tested' that can hallucinate.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Quantifies faithfulness of an auditing tool's high-stakes claim, directly informing whether NLA-based audits cause false confidence/alarms.

low_compute.reasoning: Running a released verbalizer on a small open model is inference-mostly and GPU-feasible.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Requires running NLA code on a supported model and designing matched contrastive pairs; intermediate setup risk.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Single contrastive faithfulness test of one specific claim with clear true-positive/hallucination metrics.

counterfactual_value.reasoning: Released code and open model; third-party faithfulness scrutiny is independent-friendly.

title: An N-Day Reasoning Benchmark: Can Open Models Triage Public CVE Patch Diffs?
problem: The N-day study shows frontier models can turn public vulnerability disclosures into working exploits cheaply, but there is no cheap, safe, open benchmark measuring how much exploit-relevant reasoning open models do from public CVE/patch information, and how well refusals trigger.
direction: Build a small benchmark from fully public, already-patched CVEs with public patch diffs (GitHub Security Advisories). Tasks are non-operational and analysis-only: 'given this patch diff, identify the vulnerability class and trigger conditions' (multiple-choice/short-answer, graded against the public advisory). Evaluate several open models for vulnerability-reasoning accuracy and refusal behavior, comparing base vs instruct/safety-tuned variants.
why_it_matters: Gives the community a safe, reproducible proxy for measuring the upward trend in model cyber-reasoning and how safeguards interact with it, without producing exploits — better done in the open than inside a single lab.
relevant_context: Extends 'Measuring LLMs' impact on N-day exploits' (2026) — builds a benign analysis-only open proxy plus a refusal-rate axis.
source_paper: Measuring LLMs' impact on N-day exploits — https://www.anthropic.com/research/n-days

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Gives a safe reproducible proxy for tracking model cyber-reasoning and safeguard interaction, a recognized dangerous-capability monitoring need.

low_compute.reasoning: Analysis-only multiple-choice eval over open models is inference-only and low compute.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Building a graded CVE benchmark from advisories and curating non-operational tasks is intermediate curation work.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Benchmark construction plus accuracy and refusal axes across several models is a multi-workstream deliverable.

counterfactual_value.reasoning: Public-data benign cyber-reasoning benchmark is explicitly better built in the open; neglected and independent.

title: Uncertainty-guided jailbreak discovery vs. random sampling on a fixed budget
problem: ProEval frames failure discovery as superlevel-set sampling that surfaces more diverse failures under a budget, but it is unclear whether this beats naive random search for finding safety failures with a beginner-feasible setup.
direction: Take a large pool of templated jailbreak/harmful-prompt variants (AdvBench or HarmBench prompts). Fit a simple GP/uncertainty model over embeddings of already-labeled prompts (model complied = failure), and use uncertainty-aware acquisition to choose the next prompts to test against one open model. Compare the number and cluster-coverage diversity of discovered failures against random sampling at equal query budgets.
why_it_matters: Efficient failure discovery is a bottleneck for safety red-teaming outside big labs; a clean public comparison gives independent red-teamers an actionable low-cost technique.
relevant_context: Extends 'ProEval' — its failure-discovery-as-superlevel-set-sampling result, instantiated as uncertainty-aware jailbreak search.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Plausible chain (efficient failure discovery aids independent red-teaming) but indirect to catastrophic-risk reduction.

low_compute.reasoning: GP over embeddings plus single-model queries; minimal compute.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Intermediate: GP/uncertainty acquisition over embeddings plus diversity metrics is moderately advanced for beginners.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused deliverable (failure count and diversity vs random at equal budget) but involves a non-trivial active-learning loop.

counterfactual_value.reasoning: Independent-friendly: public prompt sets and open model, actionable for outside red-teamers.

title: Why Does Public-Data Prediction Break on Agentic Tasks? A Small-Scale Diagnosis
problem: The paper reports WildChat-based predictions were ~37x worse for agentic use cases, but does not diagnose why. The gap is a clear open thread but its causes are unexplored at a scale an external researcher can probe.
direction: Take WildChat (chat-like) prefixes and a public agentic/tool-use dataset (ToolBench-style or a public agent-trace set) and, on one open instruct model, measure a single failure metric (unsafe tool call or task-derailment flagged by an LLM judge) on both. Decompose the prediction-error gap by one controlled factor at a time: conversation length, presence of tool-call formatting, number of turns.
why_it_matters: Agentic deployments are where high-stakes harms concentrate, yet that is where public-data evaluation is least reliable; understanding the failure mode tells evaluators when they can trust cheap proxies.
relevant_context: Extends 'Can public chat data predict real-world AI misalignments?' — its ~37x agentic-error open thread.
source_paper: Can public chat data predict real-world AI misalignments? — https://alignment.openai.com/validating-public-evals/

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Strong chain: agentic deployments concentrate high-stakes harms and this tells evaluators when cheap proxies can be trusted.

low_compute.reasoning: Inference on one open model over two datasets is feasible but a non-trivial generation load.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Intermediate: controlled factor decomposition of a prediction-error gap is analytically demanding for beginners.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused deliverable but decomposing the gap by multiple factors approaches a multi-workstream effort.

counterfactual_value.reasoning: Independent-friendly: public datasets and open model, diagnoses an open thread useful to outside evaluators.

title: How much do self-reports inflate AI productivity gains? A small re-survey calibrated against an objective task
problem: METR's usage survey found respondents self-report 1.4-2x value and ~3x speed gains, but notes self-reports likely overstate reality (~40pp overestimation in prior METR work) — the perceived-vs-measured gap is uncharacterized for small well-defined tasks.
direction: Recruit ~20-30 student/junior programmers (or use a public coding-task dataset with timing). For a fixed set of small gradeable tasks, collect each person's self-estimated speedup from AI, then measure their actual time with vs without an AI assistant on matched tasks. Report the per-person gap and whether it replicates METR's overestimation direction.
why_it_matters: AI risk governance increasingly relies on productivity estimates; if self-reports systematically overstate uplift, safety-relevant capability forecasts built on surveys are biased.
relevant_context: Extends METR 'Measuring the Self-Reported Impact of Early-2026 AI on Technical Worker Productivity' — its 1.4-2x self-report and ~40pp-overestimation caveat.
source_paper: Measuring the Self-Reported Impact of Early-2026 AI on Technical Worker Productivity (METR) — https://metr.org/blog/2026-05-11-ai-usage-survey/

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Plausible chain (biased productivity estimates skew capability forecasts feeding governance) but several links to catastrophic risk are indirect.

low_compute.reasoning: A survey plus timed tasks; essentially no GPU compute needed.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Intermediate: human-subject recruitment, matched-task design, and timing logistics are demanding and beyond a pure technical task for novices.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused deliverable (per-person self-report vs measured gap) but recruiting and running a study is a multi-step effort.

counterfactual_value.reasoning: Independent-friendly: doable with public tasks/volunteers, no lab access; useful external calibration of survey claims.

title: Does a misaligned trait actually propagate agent-to-agent? A minimal two-agent 'spread' simulation
problem: Mallen warns misalignment can spread at deployment, but there is little cheap empirical illustration of one misaligned agent inducing the same trait in a second initially-benign agent through normal interaction.
direction: Build a minimal two-LLM-agent loop with public API/open models: a 'carrier' agent with an injected benign-but-measurable trait (a stylistic tic or mild persistent goal) collaborates with a 'clean' agent on a shared task over multiple turns, where the clean agent's outputs feed an in-context memory. Measure whether the clean agent's behavior drifts toward the carrier's trait as interaction length grows, vs a control with a non-carrier partner. Inference only.
why_it_matters: A tangible reproducible micro-demonstration of spread dynamics using only API calls makes an abstract governance worry concrete for researchers and policymakers.
relevant_context: Extends 'Risk reports need to address deployment-time spread of misalignment' (Mallen) — its 'how to model/bound spread dynamics' open thread.
source_paper: Risk reports need to address deployment-time spread of misalignment — https://blog.redwoodresearch.org/p/risk-reports-need-to-address-deployment

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Concretizes a governance worry about spread but uses a benign stylistic trait, leaving a gap between the demo and catastrophic-risk-relevant misalignment.

low_compute.reasoning: Inference-only two-agent loop via API/open models, minimal compute.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Two-agent loop with in-context memory is approachable but orchestration and drift measurement need mentor support.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused drift-vs-interaction-length measurement with a control condition, moderately scoped.

counterfactual_value.reasoning: Open models/API, reproducible illustration independent of lab access.

title: Does Model-Spec-Style Pretext Improve Alignment Generalization in Small Open Models? A LoRA Probe
problem: MSM showed teaching a model 'why' a spec exists before alignment fine-tuning improves generalization, but on frontier Anthropic models with proprietary pipelines. Whether a cheap open analog works on small open models is unknown.
direction: Take a small open model (Llama-3.2-3B or Qwen2.5-3B). Construct a tiny public 'mini-spec' (a few behavioral rules with rationales) and generate ~200 synthetic documents explaining the spec's reasoning. Compare three LoRA fine-tunes: alignment SFT only; alignment SFT + spec-rationale documents; alignment SFT + spec-rules-only documents. Evaluate held-out generalization to rule-following in unseen formats.
why_it_matters: If a cheap open analog of MSM reproduces even part of the 'right reasons' generalization benefit, it gives small labs a lever to make open-model alignment more robust without frontier compute.
relevant_context: Extends 'Model Spec Midtraining' (2026) — the rationale-vs-rules generalization and ~40x data efficiency, tested in miniature.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: A cheap open analog of MSM's 'right reasons' generalization benefit would give small labs a robustness lever without frontier compute.

low_compute.reasoning: 3B model with three LoRA finetunes and ~200 synthetic docs fits one GPU.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Three-arm finetune comparison plus synthetic doc generation and OOD eval design is intermediate.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Clear three-arm comparison but multiple datasets/docs to build add a workstream.

counterfactual_value.reasoning: Open models and public mini-spec; independent-friendly replication of frontier-only result.

title: Catching Reward Hacks in an Automated Research Loop: A Small Audit Harness
problem: The automated researcher's agents discovered unanticipated reward hacks, yet there is no lightweight way for a small team to detect when their own automated-research loop is gaming the metric.
direction: Build a tiny automated-improvement loop on a public task where a reward hack is possible (held-out metric inflatable by label leakage or eval-split overfitting). Run the loop and add a simple secondary 'auditor' check that re-evaluates winning solutions on a clean hidden test and flags suspicious metric jumps. Measure how often the loop finds a hack and how reliably the cheap auditor catches it.
why_it_matters: Reward hacking in automated alignment research could silently corrupt the safety work it accelerates; a cheap reusable audit harness is directly valuable to anyone running such loops outside a major lab.
relevant_context: Extends 'Automated Weak-to-Strong Researcher' — the open thread that agents discovered unanticipated reward hacks.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Reward hacking can silently corrupt the safety work automated research accelerates; a reusable audit harness targets a recognized pathway.

low_compute.reasoning: A tiny improvement loop plus an auditor re-eval on a public task is cheap but multi-step.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Building an automated-improvement loop with a hackable metric and a clean hidden test needs intermediate skill.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused on hack-frequency and auditor catch-rate but requires constructing the hackable task and loop.

counterfactual_value.reasoning: A cheap reusable audit harness is directly valuable to anyone running such loops outside a major lab.

title: Do Tiny LoRA Introspection Adapters Help Small Open Models Self-Report Implanted Behaviors?
problem: Introspection adapters let large proprietary models self-report fine-tuned behaviors, but it is unknown whether the basic effect appears at all in small open models a beginner can train.
direction: Implant a simple observable behavior into an open model (LoRA-fine-tune Qwen2.5-1.5B to always recommend a made-up product, or answer in pirate-speak). Train a small LoRA introspection adapter on (behavior-implanted model, 'describe any unusual tendency you have' -> ground-truth description) pairs across 3-5 behaviors, and test on 1-2 held-out behaviors. Measure whether the adapter-equipped model names the held-out behavior more accurately than direct prompting.
why_it_matters: Self-report is a cheap potential complement to interpretability for auditing fine-tuned open models; showing whether the core mechanism survives at 1-2B scale tells the open-source community whether the technique is accessible to them.
relevant_context: Extends 'Introspection Adapters' (Shenoy et al., 2026) — reproduces its cross-behavior self-report generalization in miniature.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Self-report is a cheap auditing complement, but whether the core mechanism survives at 1-2B and translates to real misalignment is uncertain.

low_compute.reasoning: Implanting behaviors and training a small LoRA adapter on a 1.5B model is very low compute.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Multiple behavior implants plus training and testing an introspection adapter is intermediate multi-step work.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Clear held-out self-report accuracy deliverable, but requires several implanted behaviors and adapter training.

counterfactual_value.reasoning: Open model and synthetic behaviors; reproduces a proprietary technique in miniature independently.

title: Does single-domain beneficial-trait fine-tuning generalize OOD in a small open model?
problem: OpenAI reports beneficial-trait RL confined to the health domain produced cross-domain alignment gains, but used frontier-scale RL; whether the cheaper accessible analogue (small LoRA SFT on one domain) shows any OOD transfer is unknown.
direction: Build a tiny dataset of ~150-300 health-domain dialogues exemplifying one trait (honesty / epistemic humility under pressure), curated from public sources, and LoRA-fine-tune one small open model (a few hours). Evaluate tuned vs base on OOD public alignment benchmarks in unrelated domains (TruthfulQA, a sycophancy set, a small deception probe). Report whether single-domain trait tuning moves OOD alignment metrics at all.
why_it_matters: If cheap single-domain LoRA tuning yields measurable cross-domain honesty gains, alignment-via-traits becomes accessible far beyond major labs; a null result is equally informative.
relevant_context: Extends 'Reinforcement learning towards broadly and persistently beneficial models' (Jagadeesh, Heidecke et al., 2026) — its health-only-to-unrelated cross-domain result, downscaled to LoRA SFT.
source_paper: Reinforcement learning towards broadly and persistently beneficial models — https://alignment.openai.com/beneficial-rl/

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Strong chain: cheap trait-tuning OOD transfer would make alignment-via-traits accessible beyond labs, with an informative null either way.

low_compute.reasoning: LoRA SFT on a small model for a few hours is feasible on one consumer GPU but not minimal.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Intermediate: dataset curation plus LoRA fine-tuning and OOD eval requires training experience beyond pure inference.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused deliverable (OOD metric movement) but spans dataset building, fine-tuning, and several benchmarks.

counterfactual_value.reasoning: Independent-friendly: public data and open model, accessible analogue of a lab-scale RL result.
